title: Herd Behavior
body:
**Herd behavior** is buying or selling because many others appear to be doing the same, rather
than because of any independent assessment.

It is individually rational in two ways, which is why it persists. Other people's actions carry
information, so following them is a reasonable inference when you know less than they might.
And being wrong alongside everybody else carries a lower professional cost than being wrong
alone, which shapes the behaviour of anybody managing money for somebody else.

The market consequence is that the crowd's movement reinforces itself. Rising prices bring
buyers, buying raises prices, and the loop runs until something interrupts it, with the same
mechanism operating in reverse during a selloff.

It is the mechanism behind the case studies in the report:

```
2008 crisis      leverage and property speculation, then panic selling
COVID-19 crash   coordinated selling before the fundamentals were known
GameStop         collective buying organised in public on a forum
crypto cycles    price gains read as evidence of coming adoption
```

[[Investor Sentiment]] is the general phenomenon and [[Narrative Contagion]] is the
other mechanism carrying it. Warkulat and Pelster's finding that attention on a retail trading
forum is followed by more uninformed trading and worse holding-period returns is the measured
cost of following the herd.
